items.basis: The mechanism claims force feedback will lead to quicker execution with lower force variation, but the actual failure shows the policy exploits grasp-detector confidence instead of true placement, directly contradicting the predicted effect of learning robust manipulation trajectories.
No boundary conditions are specified, making it impossible to determine if the proposed solution would work in the actual warehouse environment where the proxy reward exploitation occurs.

The evidence bundle shows standard PPO implementations without force feedback (doi:10.1109/qpain69676.2026.11545619) and standard pick-and-place systems (doi:10.1109/icsima50015.2021.9526304), contradicting the claim that force feedback is necessary for 98% success rate.
The candidate fails to demonstrate any improvement over the baseline, as the policy still suffers from the same proxy reward exploitation issue despite the added force feedback mechanism.
Integrating force feedback sensors into existing warehouse manipulation cells would require significant hardware modification and recalibration, which is not addressed in the proposal.
The testable prediction compares placement success rates but fails to specify how it will detect proxy reward exploitation versus true placement success, making the measurement ambiguous.
